newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour may seek tighter rules on alcohol ads.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour may seek tighter rules on alcohol ads.

text.p: Britain's Labour Party, if it wins the next election, may tighten rules on advertising alcohol products aimed at young people, an industry spokesman said on Tuesday.

John Hooper, director general of the Incorporated Society of British Advertisers (ISBA), said Nigel Griffiths, Labour's shadow consumer affairs minister, made the comment in a meeting on Monday with industry representatives.

Hooper told Reuters Griffiths discussed alcohol, tobacco and toy advertising, ads on the Internet and other advertising-related topics with about 50 executives from brand-name companies, ad agencies and media groups.

He said Griffiths said Labour would not hesitate to bring in legislate to regulate advertising of something like Britain's new "alcopops", fruit-flavoured alcoholic drinks, if self-regulation was not seen to be working.

The Portman Group, a body funded by seven leading brewers and distillers, is meant to promote sensible drinking and ensure, among other things, that alcohol is not being marketed to underage drinkers.
"(Griffiths said) he wanted to take a look at the 'alcopops' and wanted to see how the Portman Group's own code was working," Hooper said.
"It was not an area he would hesitate to move into," Hooper said.
He quoted Griffiths as telling the group on Monday "We will not hesitate to legislate if (self-regulation) does not work".
The purpose of the meeting was for the Labour Party to get to know members of the advertising industry and discuss important issues facing the industry.
Many people in the advertising industry have said they were worried any future Labour government would be "anti-advertising".
Hooper said it was a productive meeting.

He said Griffiths said Britain's Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), the self-regulatory body that oversees non-broadcast advertising, was doing a good job but needed greater powers to punish repeat offenders in the advertising field.
Griffiths told the group any future Labour government would ban tobacco advertising, a position the industry is already familiar with.
